G0082.d:
APT38 is a North Korean state-sponsored threat group that specializes in financial cyber operations; it has been attributed to the Reconnaissance General Bureau. Active since at least 2014, APT38 has targeted banks, financial institutions, casinos, cryptocurrency exchanges, SWIFT system endpoints, and ATMs in at least 38 countries worldwide. Significant operations include the 2016 Bank of Bangladesh heist, Bancomext and Banco de Chile , along with software supply chain compromises and destructive malware attacks.

North Korean group definitions are known to have significant overlap, and some security researchers report all North Korean state-sponsored cyber activity under the name Lazarus Group instead of tracking clusters or subgroups.

pr.p: APT38 has collected data from a compromised host.
APT38 has run node.js malware to query the Registry to discover installed software.
APT38 has used several code packing methods such as Themida, Enigma, VMProtect, and Obsidium, to pack their implants.
APT38 has utilized Base64 encoded PowerShell scripts.
APT38 has compressed its malicious payloads in ZIP files for delivery to victims.
APT38 has added thousands of blank lines to scripts to push malicious logic past the scrollable view of the script editor.
APT38 has identified primary users, currently logged in users, sets of users that commonly use a system, or inactive users. APT38 has run malware to enumerate the current user on compromised hosts.
APT38 has renamed system utilities, such as `rundll32.exe` and `mshta.exe`, to avoid detection.

tech.n: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

pr.p: APT38 has named malicious payloads as benign-looking executables to blend in the environment including Run keys, npm packages, and JavaScript utilities often using names mirroring Apple, Windows, or other native system files.
APT38 has put several spaces before a file extension to avoid detection and suspicion.
APT38 has configured malware to rename malicious payloads with naming conventions that reduce a chance of detection to include renaming “package.md” to “package.json”.
APT38 has exfiltrated victim device and user details contained in a POST request to register the compromised system with C2 infrastructure.

tech.n: Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol

pr.p: APT38 has used malware to exfiltrate stolen data with a custom ICAP-style protocol over HTTPS.
APT38 installed a port monitoring tool, MAPMAKER, to print the active TCP connections on the local system.
APT38 has used cron to create pre-scheduled and periodic background jobs on a Linux system.

APT38 has used Task Scheduler to run programs at system startup or on a scheduled basis for persistence. Additionally, APT38 has used living-off-the-land scripts to execute a malicious script via a scheduled task.
APT38 has used a multiplatform implant that can write to `~/.config/systemd/nvmconf/` to gain persistence on Linux hosts.
APT38 has injected malicious payloads into the `explorer.exe` process. APT38 has also injected malicious binaries directly into memory on compromised hosts.
APT38 used a Trojan called KEYLIME to capture keystrokes from the victim’s machine.
APT38 has leveraged a fictitious native macOS password dialog prompt to entice victims to enter credentials.

APT38 leveraged Sysmon to understand the processes, services in the organization. APT38 has used Python versions of its remote access tools on Linux targets. APT38 has also configured malicious payloads to gather running processes using `ps aux`.

APT38 has used PowerShell to execute commands and other operational tasks.
APT38 has also used PowerShell to establish persistence and establish C2 communication on compromised hosts.

APT38 has sent Mac users.scpt files to trigger malicious downloads. APT38 has targeted macOS uses with native script stagers leading to malicious paylaods. APT38 has also used an AppleScript-based credential harvesting component.

APT38 has used a command-line tunneler, NACHOCHEESE, to give them shell access to a victim’s machine. Additionally, APT38 has used batch scripts. APT38 has also executed scripts to launch `cmd.exe` to POST stolen data to actor-controlled domains.
APT38 has run malicious payloads using Linux and Unix shells. APT38 has also executed Unix commands sequentially using `&&` and in the background with `&`.

APT38 has used VBScript to execute commands and other operational tasks. APT38 has sent Windows victims Visual Basic script stagers leading to malicious downloads. APT38 has also used VBScript to execute scripts for data exfiltration.
APT38 has used Python versions of its remote access tools on Linux targets.
APT38 has utilized malicious JavaScript payloads to compromise victims.
APT38 has executed scripts to delete the PowerShell command history file.

APT38 has used a utility called CLOSESHAVE that can securely delete a file from the system. APT38 has also removed malware, tools, scripts, or other non-native files used during the intrusion to reduce their footprint or as part of the post-intrusion cleanup process.
APT38 has modified data timestamps to mimic files that are in the same folder on a compromised host.

APT38 used a backdoor, QUICKRIDE, to communicate to the C2 server over HTTP and HTTPS. APT38 has also configured malicious payloads to communicate with C2 using HTTP POST requests that blend in with common traffic.
APT38 has staged files in a central location prior to exfiltration.
APT38 has validated stolen credentials against the local macOS authentication database using directory services prior to exfiltration.
APT38 has used victim maintainer accounts for the npm Registry to publish malicious packages.

APT38 has attempted to get detailed information about a compromised host, including the operating system, version, patches, hotfixes, and service packs. APT38 has executed malware to collect current user, host name, system time, and operating system install date from targeted systems.
APT38 has enumerated files and directories, or searched in specific locations within a compromised host.

APT38 used a backdoor, NESTEGG, that has the capability to download and upload files to and from a victim’s machine. Additionally, APT38 has downloaded other payloads onto a victim’s machine. APT38 has also injected npm packages with malicious dependencies that download second-stage payloads to victim machines.
APT38 has used the Windows API to execute code within a victim's system.
APT38 has used brute force techniques to attempt account access when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are unavailable.
APT38 uses a tool called CLEANTOAD that has the capability to modify Registry keys.
APT38 used a Trojan called KEYLIME to collect data from the clipboard.
APT38 has run malware to discover the system time on compromised hosts.
APT38 has utilized Base64 encoded HTTP POST communications to C2.
APT38 has enumerated network shares on a compromised host.
APT38 has used the RC4 algorithm to decrypt configuration data. APT38 has decocoded Base64 encoded PowerShell scripts prior to execution.
APT38 has conducted watering holes schemes to gain initial access to victims.

tech.n: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools

pr.p: APT38 has injected malicious dependencies into software packages such as Axios and Mastra npm packages.
APT38 has used links to execute a malicious Visual Basic script. APT38 has directed users to navigate to a website under adversary control through the sharing of links in messages.

APT38 has attempted to lure victims into enabling malicious macros within email attachments. Additionally, APT38 has used malicious Word documents and shortcut files. APT38 has lured victims into opening malicious .scpt or .vbs files to fix fake connection issues with online meetings. APT38 has used social media invites to lure victims into opening malicious files hosted on cloud infrastructure.

APT38 has gathered Telegram Desktop messaging data from the applications data directories stored on the victim device to include cryptographic key material, and session mapping files that can recreate a compromised user’s Telegram session on another system.
APT38 has copied Apple Notes database from its application container and staged for upload.

APT38 has collected browser bookmark information to learn more about compromised hosts, obtain personal information about users, and acquire details about internal network resources. APT38 has also used malware capable of enumerating 166 unique cryptocurrency wallets, browser extensions, and browser history.
APT38 has used CHM files to move concealed payloads.
c: Kaspersky Lazarus Under The Hood APR 2017

pr.p: APT38 has used a renamed version of `mshta.exe` to execute malicious HTML files.
APT38 has used `msiexec.exe` to execute malicious files.
APT38 has used rundll32.exe to execute binaries, scripts, and Control Panel Item files and to execute code via proxy to avoid triggering security tools.
APT38 has changed file and directory permissions using `chmod 777`.
APT38 has leveraged file discovery actions to determine if a predetermined file is present prior to execution to prevent redundant execution on a compromised device.
APT38 has created a mutex to avoid duplicate execution.
APT38 has used a custom secure delete function to make deleted files unrecoverable.
APT38 has used Hermes ransomware to encrypt files with AES256.
APT38 has used web shells for persistence or to ensure redundant access.
APT38 has enumerated installed applications to build an inventory of the system’s software environment.

APT38 has identified security software, configurations, defensive tools, and sensors installed on a compromised system. APT38 has also executed malware implants to enumerate all installed applications on Windows hosts including installed security products.
APT38 has used a custom MBR wiper named BOOTWRECK, which will initiate a system reboot after wiping the victim's MBR.
APT38 has executed a multiplatform implant that placed launch agents in ~/Library/NodePackages/ to establish persistence on macOS.

APT38 has installed a new Windows service to establish persistence. APT38 has gained persistence on compromised systems independent of user logon by creating a background service using `sc create scdev binPath= "c:\windows\system32\svchost.exe -k scdev".
APT38 has established persistence through storing the malicious plist files in `/Library/LaunchDaemons`.
APT38 has poisoned Axios and Mastra npm packages with malicious post-install hooks.

APT38 has also added registry run keys within `HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\MicrosoftUpdate` to enable persistence on Windows devices after reboot. APT38 has executed a multiplatform implant that dropped a Registry Run key to `:\ProgramData\NodePackages\` for persistence on Windows machines. APT38 has obtained boot- persistence on compromised systems independent of user logon by adding the registry key `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\services\scdev\Parameters`.
APT38 has used the legitimate application `ieinstal.exe` to bypass UAC.
APT38 has executed persistence actions using `sudo` commands within zsh shells.

APT38 has used Finder, a macOS native app with FDA permissions, to rename the folder `com.apple.TCC`, then used another process to move the `TCC.db` file to a new location, where SQLite3 was used to edit `TCC.db`. The edited `TCC.db` file allowed code signing authorization, permission access, etc. without requiring a user prompt.
APT38 has gathered data and credentials stored in Shell History.
APT38 has gathered cryptographic key data related to cryptocurrency wallets, SSH keys, and messaging applications to include Telegram.
APT38 has used ISO and VHD files to deploy malware and to bypass Mark-of-the-Web (MOTW) security measures.
APT38 has stolen credentials from the compromised device to include those used to access cryptocurrency wallets.
APT38 has stolen data stored in macOS keychain.
APT38 has gathered Web browser data to include saved credentials, cookies, bookmarks, autofill data, and extension-specific storage. APT38 has also sought cryptocurrency wallet extensions.
APT38 has archived collected data within ZIP files prior to exfiltration.
APT38 has used a custom MBR wiper named BOOTWRECK to render systems inoperable.
APT38 has configured malicious scripts to execute in hidden windows.
APT38 has used remote access tools that run AppleScript using ` nohup osascript` to ignore hangup signals.
APT38 has added Microsoft Defender exclusions to include `C:\Windows\System32` to suppress detection of dropped tooling.
APT38 has used DYEPACK to create, delete, and alter records in databases used for SWIFT transactions.
APT38 has used DYEPACK to manipulate SWIFT messages en route to a printer.
APT38 has used DYEPACK.FOX to manipulate PDF data as it is accessed to remove traces of fraudulent SWIFT transactions from the data displayed to the end user.
APT38 has conducted spearphishing campaigns using malicious email attachments. APT38 has sent fake Zoom support emails with malicious attachments.
APT38 has sent phishing emails with invite links to fictitious meetings.
APT38 has used social media sites such as LinkedIn to send malicious links to potential vicitims.
APT38 has exfiltrated stolen credentials to actor-controlled infrastructure leveraging Telegram Bot API.
APT38 has created new services or modified existing ones to run executables, commands, or scripts. APT38 has also installed a persistent service on targeted hosts to load malicious DLLs at boot.
APT38 has leveraged unique non-standard ports for communications with actor-controlled C2 infrastructure to include Port 8000.

APT38 has created fake domains to imitate legitimate venture capital or bank domains. APT38 has acquired domains to host fake skill assessments leading to malware download. APT38 has registered domains that masquerade as financial institutions and resemble legitimate services. APT38 has also obtained C2 domains to host second-stage malicious payloads.
APT38 has used virtual private server (VPS) providers to host C2 infrastructure including Hostwinds.
APT38 has used OneDrive and GoogleDrive to host malicious files.
APT38 has used professional platforms such as LinkedIn to contact potential victims.
APT38 has set up anonymous emails to use in publishing poisoned software packages such as sergey2016@tutamail[.]com.
APT38 has used virtual private server (VPS) providers to host C2 infrastructure including Hostwinds.
APT38 has obtained and used open-source tools such as Mimikatz.
APT38 has uploaded malware to cloud storage services for download by targeted victims.

APT38 has configured malicious payloads to reflectively load using the macOS `NSCreateObjectFileImageFromMemory` API.
APT38 has also reflectively loaded .NET DLLs to bypass disk-based detection.
APT38 has conducted cryptocurrency theft.

APT38 has poisoned npm packages with fake runtime dependencies to trigger execution of malicious payloads on developer endpoints or continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) systems during npm installation or update.
APT38 has delayed C2 beaconing to longer intervals on network failures.
APT38 has created decoy content that resembles legitimate guidance for support to victims that contain hidden malicious actions.
APT38 has created fictitious profiles on social media utilizing fake photos and personas to entice users to engage in the schemes.
APT38 has impersonated recruiters and venture capitalists to lure victims into connecting to malicious skills assessments or online business meetings.
APT38 has unhooked DLLs to disable endpoint detection and response (EDR) or anti-virus (AV) tools.
APT38 has displayed a fake “system update complete” dialog to the user following successful deployment of malicious payloads.
APT38 clears Window Event logs and Sysmon logs from the system.
APT38 have created firewall exemptions on specific ports, including ports 443, 6443, 8443, and 9443.
APT38 have created firewall exemptions on specific ports, including ports 443, 6443, 8443, and 9443.

APT38 has prepended a space to all of their terminal commands to operate without leaving traces in the HISTCONTROL environment.
APT38 has prevented logging and muted error logs through the use of `/dev/null 2>&1 &`. 
APT38 has also executed scripts to delete the PowerShell command history file and to prevent future history recording using `-Force Set-PSReadLineOption -HistorySaveStyle SaveNothing`.

G0119.d: Indrik Spider is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since at least 2014. Indrik Spider initially started with the Dridex banking Trojan, and then by 2017 they began running ransomware operations using BitPaymer, WastedLocker, and Hades ransomware. Following U.S. sanctions and an indictment in 2019, Indrik Spider changed their tactics and diversified their toolset.

pr.p: Indrik Spider used Cobalt Strike to carry out credential dumping using ProcDump.
Indrik Spider has used the win32_service WMI class to retrieve a list of services from the system.
Indrik Spider has used a service account to extract copies of the `Security` Registry hive.
Indrik Spider has used PowerView to enumerate all Windows Server, Windows Server 2003, and Windows 7 instances in the Active Directory database.
Indrik Spider has used RDP for lateral movement.
Indrik Spider has used SSH for lateral movement.

tech.n: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

pr.p: Indrik Spider used fake updates for FlashPlayer plugin and Google Chrome as initial infection vectors.
Indrik Spider has used WMIC to execute commands on remote computers.
Indrik Spider has used PowerShell Empire for execution of malware.
Indrik Spider has used batch scripts on victim's machines.
Indrik Spider has used malicious JavaScript files for several components of their attack.
Indrik Spider has stored collected data in a .tmp file.
Indrik Spider has used valid accounts for initial access and lateral movement. Indrik Spider has also maintained access to the victim environment through the VPN infrastructure.
Indrik Spider has collected credentials from infected systems, including domain accounts.
Indrik Spider has downloaded additional scripts, malware, and tools onto a compromised host.
Indrik Spider has modified registry keys to prepare for ransomware execution and to disable common administrative utilities.
Indrik Spider used wmic.exe to add a new user to the system.
Indrik Spider has created local system accounts and has added the accounts to privileged groups.
Indrik Spider has attempted to get users to click on a malicious zipped file.
Indrik Spider has used Group Policy Objects to deploy batch scripts.
Indrik Spider has encrypted domain-controlled systems using BitPaymer. Additionally, Indrik Spider used PsExec to execute a ransomware script.
Indrik Spider has used PsExec to stop services prior to the execution of ransomware.
Indrik Spider has searched files to obtain and exfiltrate credentials.
Indrik Spider has accessed and exported passwords from password managers.
Indrik Spider has conducted Kerberoasting attacks using a module from GitHub.
Indrik Spider has exfiltrated data using Rclone or MEGASync prior to deploying ransomware.
Indrik Spider has purchased access to victim VPNs to facilitate access to victim environments.
Indrik Spider has served fake updates via legitimate websites that have been compromised.
Indrik Spider has created email accounts to communicate with their ransomware victims, to include providing payment and decryption details.
Indrik Spider has developed malware for their operations, including ransomware such as BitPaymer and WastedLocker.

Indrik Spider has downloaded tools, such as the Advanced Port Scanner utility and Lansweeper, to conduct internal reconnaissance of the victim network. Indrik Spider has also accessed the victim’s VMware VCenter, which had information about host configuration, clusters, etc.

Indrik Spider used PsExec to leverage Windows Defender to disable scanning of all downloaded files and to restrict real-time monitoring. Indrik Spider has used `MpCmdRun` to revert the definitions in Microsoft Defender. Additionally, Indrik Spider has used WMI to stop or uninstall and reset anti-virus products and other defensive services.
Indrik Spider has used Cobalt Strike to empty log files. Additionally, Indrik Spider has cleared all event logs using `wevutil`.

G0055.d: NEODYMIUM is an activity group that conducted a campaign in May 2016 and has heavily targeted Turkish victims. The group has demonstrated similarity to another activity group called PROMETHIUM due to overlapping victim and campaign characteristics. NEODYMIUM is reportedly associated closely with BlackOasis operations, but evidence that the group names are aliases has not been identified.

G1043.d: BlackByte is a ransomware threat actor operating since at least 2021. BlackByte is associated with several versions of ransomware also labeled BlackByte Ransomware. BlackByte ransomware operations initially used a common encryption key allowing for the development of a universal decryptor, but subsequent versions such as BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware use more robust encryption mechanisms. BlackByte is notable for operations targeting critical infrastructure entities among other targets across North America.

pr.p: BlackByte used tools such as Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz to dump credentials from victim systems.
BlackByte queried registry values to determine system language settings.
BlackByte used tools such as Arp to pull system network information and identify connected devices.
BlackByte used tools such as Arp to identify remotely-connected devices.
BlackByte has used RDP to access other hosts within victim networks.
BlackByte used SMB file shares to distribute payloads throughout victim networks, including BlackByte ransomware variants during wormable operations.
BlackByte masqueraded configuration files containing encryption keys as PNG files.
BlackByte transmitted collected victim host information via HTTP POST to command and control infrastructure.
BlackByte has used tools such as NetScan to enumerate network services in victim environments.
BlackByte used WMI to delete Volume Shadow Copies on victim machines.
BlackByte created scheduled tasks for payload execution.
BlackByte has injected Cobalt Strike into `wuauclt.exe` during intrusions. BlackByte has injected ransomware into `svchost.exe` before encryption.
BlackByte used process hollowing for defense evasion purposes.
BlackByte used encoded PowerShell commands during operations. BlackByte has used remote PowerShell commands in victim networks.
BlackByte executed ransomware using the Windows command shell.
BlackByte has exploited CVE-2024-37085 in VMWare ESXi software for authentication bypass and subsequent privilege escalation.
BlackByte deleted ransomware executables post-encryption.
BlackByte collected victim device information then transmitted this via HTTP POST to command and control infrastructure.
BlackByte has gained access to victim environments through legitimate VPN credentials.
BlackByte captured credentials for or impersonated domain administration users.
BlackByte used various system commands and tools to pull system information during operations.
BlackByte has used tools such as AdFind to identify and enumerate domain accounts.
BlackByte has transferred tools such as Cobalt Strike to victim environments from file sharing and hosting websites.
BlackByte performed Registry modifications to escalate privileges and disable security tools.
BlackByte constructed a valid authentication token following Microsoft Exchange exploitation to allow for follow-on privileged command execution.
BlackByte enumerated network shares on victim devices.
BlackByte created privileged domain accounts during intrusions.
BlackByte has encoded commands in base64-encoded sections concatenated together in PowerShell. BlackByte uses PowerShell commands to disable Windows Defender.
BlackByte exploited vulnerabilities such as ProxyLogon and ProxyShell for initial access to victim environments.
BlackByte has used tools such as AnyDesk in victim environments.

BlackByte stopped execution if identified language settings on victim machines was Russian or one of several language associated with former Soviet republics. BlackByte has used ransomware variants requiring a key passed on the command line for the malware to execute.
BlackByte enumerated Active Directory information and trust relationships during operations.
BlackByte has encrypted victim files for ransom. Early versions of BlackByte ransomware used a common key for encryption, but later versions use unique keys per victim.
BlackByte resized and deleted volume shadow copy files to prevent system recovery after encryption.
BlackByte left ransom notes in all directories where encryption takes place.
BlackByte has used ASPX web shells following exploitation of vulnerabilities in services such as Microsoft Exchange.
BlackByte enumerated installed security products during operations.
BlackByte modified multiple services on victim machines to enable encryption operations. BlackByte has installed tools such as AnyDesk as a service on victim machines.
BlackByte has used Registry Run keys for persistence.
BlackByte compressed data collected from victim environments prior to exfiltration.
BlackByte has used services such as `anonymfiles.com` and `file.io` to exfiltrate victim data.
BlackByte created malicious services for ransomware execution.
BlackByte transfered tools such as Cobalt Strike and the AnyDesk remote access tool during operations using SMB shares.
BlackByte staged encryption keys on virtual private servers operated by the adversary.
BlackByte has staged tools such as Cobalt Strike at public file sharing and hosting sites.
BlackByte identified system language settings to determine follow-on execution.
BlackByte disabled security tools such as Windows Defender and the Raccine anti-ransomware tool during operations.
BlackByte modified firewall rules on victim machines to enable remote system discovery.

sw.p: BlackByte has used Cobalt Strike as a post-exploitation tool.
BlackByte Ransomware is ransomware uniquely associated with BlackByte operations prior to 2023.
BlackByte has used Mimikatz for credential dumping during operations.
BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware is ransomware uniquely associated with BlackByte operations and is a replacement for BlackByte Ransomware.
BlackByte used Exbyte for automated file collection and exfiltration.
BlackByte used AdFind during operations.
BlackByte has used PsExec to remotely execute payloads during wormable ransomware execution.
BlackByte used Arp to identify connected hosts in victim networks.

G0066.d: Elderwood is a suspected Chinese cyber espionage group that was reportedly responsible for the 2009 Google intrusion known as Operation Aurora. The group has targeted defense organizations, supply chain manufacturers, human rights and nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), and IT service providers.

pr.p: Elderwood has packed malware payloads before delivery to victims.
Elderwood has encrypted documents and malicious executables.
The Ritsol backdoor trojan used by Elderwood can download files onto a compromised host from a remote location.
Elderwood has delivered zero-day exploits and malware to victims by injecting malicious code into specific public Web pages visited by targets within a particular sector.
Elderwood has used exploitation of endpoint software, including Microsoft Internet Explorer Adobe Flash vulnerabilities, to gain execution. They have also used zero-day exploits.
Elderwood has leveraged multiple types of spearphishing in order to attempt to get a user to open links.
Elderwood has leveraged multiple types of spearphishing in order to attempt to get a user to open attachments.
Elderwood has delivered zero-day exploits and malware to victims via targeted emails containing malicious attachments.

G0093.d: GALLIUM is a cyberespionage group that has been active since at least 2012, primarily targeting telecommunications companies, financial institutions, and government entities in Afghanistan, Australia, Belgium, Cambodia, Malaysia, Mozambique, the Philippines, Russia, and Vietnam. This group is particularly known for launching Operation Soft Cell, a long-term campaign targeting telecommunications providers. Security researchers have identified GALLIUM as a likely Chinese state-sponsored group, based in part on tools used and TTPs commonly associated with Chinese threat actors.

pr.p: GALLIUM used a modified version of Mimikatz along with a PowerShell-based Mimikatz to dump credentials on the victim machines.
GALLIUM used reg commands to dump specific hives from the Windows Registry, such as the SAM hive, and obtain password hashes.
GALLIUM collected data from the victim's local system, including password hashes from the SAM hive in the Registry.
GALLIUM used ipconfig /all to obtain information about the victim network configuration. The group also ran a modified version of NBTscan to identify available NetBIOS name servers.
GALLIUM used a modified version of NBTscan to identify available NetBIOS name servers over the network as well as ping to identify remote systems.
GALLIUM used a modified version of HTRAN in which they obfuscated strings such as debug messages in an apparent attempt to evade detection.
GALLIUM packed some payloads using different types of packers, both known and custom.
GALLIUM ensured each payload had a unique hash, including by using different types of packers.
GALLIUM used whoami and query user to obtain information about the victim user.
GALLIUM used a renamed cmd.exe file to evade detection.
GALLIUM used Web shells and HTRAN for C2 and to exfiltrate data.
GALLIUM used WMI for execution to assist in lateral movement as well as for installing tools across multiple assets.
GALLIUM used netstat -oan to obtain information about the victim network connections.
GALLIUM established persistence for PoisonIvy by created a scheduled task.
GALLIUM used PowerShell for execution to assist in lateral movement as well as for dumping credentials stored on compromised machines.
GALLIUM used the Windows command shell to execute commands.
GALLIUM compressed and staged files in multi-part archives in the Recycle Bin prior to exfiltration.
GALLIUM leveraged valid accounts to maintain access to a victim network.
GALLIUM used a modified version of HTRAN to redirect connections between networks.
GALLIUM dropped additional tools to victims during their operation, including portqry.exe, a renamed cmd.exe file, winrar, and HTRAN.
GALLIUM has used VPN services, including SoftEther VPN, to access and maintain persistence in victim environments.
GALLIUM created high-privileged domain user accounts to maintain access to victim networks.
GALLIUM exploited a publicly-facing servers including Wildfly/JBoss servers to gain access to the network.
GALLIUM used Web shells to persist in victim environments and assist in execution and exfiltration.
GALLIUM used dumped hashes to authenticate to other machines via pass the hash.
GALLIUM has used stolen certificates to sign its tools including those from Whizzimo LLC.
GALLIUM used WinRAR to compress and encrypt stolen data prior to exfiltration.
GALLIUM has used PsExec to move laterally between hosts in the target network.
GALLIUM used DLL side-loading to covertly load PoisonIvy into memory on the victim machine.
GALLIUM has used Taiwan-based servers that appear to be exclusive to GALLIUM.
GALLIUM has used a variety of widely-available tools, which in some cases they modified to add functionality and/or subvert antimalware solutions.

G0094.d:
Kimsuky is a Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK)-based cyber espionage group that has been active since at least 2012. The group initially targeted South Korean government agencies, think tanks, and subject-matter experts in various fields. Its operations expanded to include the United Nations and organizations in the government, education, business services, and manufacturing sectors across the United States, Japan, Russia, and Europe. Kimsuky has focused collection on foreign policy and national security issues tied to the Korean Peninsula, nuclear policy, and sanctions. Kimsuky operations have overlapped with those of other North Korean state-sponsored cyber espionage actors as a result of ad hoc collaborations or other limited resource sharing. 

Kimsuky was assessed to be responsible for the 2014 Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power Co. compromise; other notable campaigns include Operation STOLEN PENCIL (2018), Operation Kabar Cobra (2019), and Operation Smoke Screen (2019). In 2023, Kimsuky was observed using commercial large language models (LLMs) to assist with vulnerability research, scripting, social engineering and reconnaissance.

DPRK threat actor cluster boundaries overlap in open source reporting, with some security researchers consolidating all attributed North Korean state-sponsored cyber activity under Lazarus Group, rather than tracking operationally distinct subgroups.

pr.p: Kimsuky has gathered credentials using Mimikatz and ProcDump.

Kimsuky has collected Office, PDF, and HWP documents from its victims. Kimsuky has also harvested victim files through the use of the `RecentFiles()` function that collects paths of recently accessed files by parsing .lnk shortcuts from `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Recent`.
Kimsuky has used an instrumentor script to gather the names of all services running on a victim's system.
Kimsuky has obtained specific Registry keys and values on a compromised host.

Kimsuky has used `ipconfig/all` and web beacons sent via email to gather network configuration information. Kimsuky has also identified Host IP addresses leveraging the WMI class `Win32_NetworkAdapterConfiguration`.
Kimsuky has exfiltrated data to C2 servers using an automated script that executes every 10 minutes and after successful checks for the presence of pre-designated staged filenames.
Kimsuky has used RDP for direct remote point-and-click access.

Kimsuky has obfuscated binary strings including the use of XOR encryption and Base64 encoding. Kimsuky has also modified the first byte of DLL implants targeting victims to prevent recognition of the executable file format. Kimsuky has obfuscated strings using Single Instruction Multiple Data (SIMD) instructions that complicate static analysis.
Kimsuky has performed padding of PowerShell command line code with over 100 spaces.
Kimsuky has packed malware with UPX.
Kimsuky has leveraged dynamic API resolution using custom hashing techniques.
Kimsuky has encoded malicious PowerShell scripts using Base64.
Kimsuky has used the LNK icon location to execute malicious scripts. Kimsuky has also padded the LNK target field properties with extra spaces to obscure the script.

Kimsuky has obfuscated code within files by converting hexadecimal strings to decimal numbers using the `CLng function` in combination with processing arithmetic operations and leveraging the `Chr function` to generate readable characters. Kimsuky has also encoded files with Base64 and RC4. Kimsuky has utilized XOR and RC4 to encode malicious payloads.
Kimsuky has delivered malicious payloads within Zip archives.
Kimsuky has obfuscated code by filling scripts with junk code and concatenating strings to hamper analysis and detection.
Kimsuky has gathered the identity of the user by querying `System.Security.Principal` namespace using the `GetCurrent()` method.
Kimsuky has disguised services to appear as benign software or related to operating system functions.

tech.n: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

pr.p: Kimsuky has renamed malware to legitimate names such as ESTCommon.dll or patch.dll. Kimsuky has also disguised payloads using legitimate file names including a PowerShell payload named chrome.ps1. Kimsuky has also used a malicious QR code that masqueraded as a legitimate package delivery service.
Kimsuky has used an additional filename extension to hide the true file type. Kimsuky has also masqueraded malicious LNK files as PDF objects using the double extension .pdf.lnk.
Kimsuky has used the Nirsoft SniffPass network sniffer to obtain passwords sent over non-secure protocols.
Kimsuky has exfiltrated data over its C2 channel.

Kimsuky has downloaded additional malware with scheduled tasks. Kimsuky has established persistence by creating a scheduled task named “ChromeUpdateTaskMachine” through the PowerShell cmdlet `Register-ScheduleTask` which was set to execute another PowerShell script once, then five minutes after its creation and periodically repeat every 30 minutes. Kimsuky has also set scheduled tasks that run periodically using the PT1M repetition pattern leveraging naming conventions of Anti-Virus software to include "AhnlabUpdate".
Kimsuky has used Win7Elevate to inject malicious code into explorer.exe.

Kimsuky has the ability to load DLLs via reflective injection by allocating memory using `VirtualAllocEx()`, then decrypting a DLL with `WriteProcessMemory()` and invoking execution through `CreateRemoteThread()`.
Kimsuky has used a file injector DLL to spawn a benign process on the victim's system and inject the malicious payload into it via process hollowing.

Kimsuky has used a PowerShell-based keylogger as well as a tool called MECHANICAL to log keystrokes. Kimsuky has also leveraged Native Windows API functions such as `GetAsyncKeyState()` along with others to capture keystrokes every 50 milliseconds and stores data in a file stored in the temp directory.
Kimsuky has collected credentials from a fake Google account login page.
Kimsuky can gather a list of all processes running on a victim's machine. Kimsuky has also obtained running processes on the victim device utilizing PowerShell cmdlet `Get-Process`.

Kimsuky has executed a variety of PowerShell scripts including Invoke-Mimikatz. Kimsuky has also utilized PowerShell scripts for execution, persistence, and defense evasion. Kimsuky has leveraged PowerShell’s cmdlet `Expand-Archive` to extract contents of zip files into the same directory. Kimsuky has employed ClickFix type tactics enticing victims to copy and paste malicious PowerShell commands and scripts, where the scripts ultimately led to QuasarRAT.

Kimsuky has executed Windows commands by using `cmd` and running batch scripts. Kimsuky has also used `cmd.exe` to automatically open downloaded decoy pdf documents with the system’s default PDF viewer. Kimsuky has utilized malicious payloads to create reverse shells within the victim environment. Kimsuky has also used batch scripts to eventually run QuasarRAT.

Kimsuky has used Visual Basic to download malicious payloads. Kimsuky has also used malicious VBA macros within maldocs disguised as forms that trigger when a victim types any content into the lure. Kimsuky has also leveraged VBScript (VBS) scripts to execute temp.vbs every 19 minutes using a scheduled task to run QuasarRAT.
Kimsuky has used a macOS Python implant to gather data as well as MailFetcher.py code to automatically collect email data.

Kimsuky has used JScript for logging and downloading additional tools. Kimsuky has used TRANSLATEXT, which contained four Javascript files for bypassing defenses, collecting sensitive information and screenshots, and exfiltrating data.

Kimsuky has deleted the exfiltrated data on disk after transmission. Kimsuky has also used an instrumentor script to terminate browser processes running on an infected system and then delete the cookie files on disk. Kimsuky has deleted files using the `Remove-Item` PowerShell commandlet to remove traces of executed payloads. Kimsuky has also removed remnants of files used for delivery to include .log and .zip files.
Kimsuky has manipulated timestamps for creation or compilation dates to defeat anti-forensics.
Kimsuky has used HTTP GET and POST requests for C2.
Kimsuky has used FTP to download additional malware to the target machine.
Kimsuky has used e-mail to send exfiltrated data to C2 servers.

Kimsuky has staged collected data files under C:\Program Files\Common Files\System\Ole DB\. Kimsuky has also gathered data in structured directories prior to exfiltration under the %TEMP% environment variable.
Kimsuky has used a tool called GREASE to add a Windows admin account in order to allow them continued access via RDP.

Kimsuky has enumerated OS type, OS version, and other information using a script or the "systeminfo" command. Kimsuky has also obtained system information such as OS type, OS version, and system type through querying various Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) classes including `Win32_OperatingSystem`.

Kimsuky has the ability to enumerate all files and directories on an infected system. Kimsuky has used a custom script with a function called CreateFileList() that can scan all filesystem drives, prioritizing C:\Users, to locate files and file extensions of interest that ultimately generates a file called `FileList.txt` saved within the victims %TEMP% Directory that contains the findings and the respective pathways.
Kimsuky has added accounts to specific groups with net localgroup.
Kimsuky has used TRANSLATEXT and a dead drop resolver to retrieve configurations and commands from a public blog site.
Kimsuky has used Blogspot pages and a Github repository for C2. Kimsuky has also leveraged Dropbox for downloading payloads and uploading victim system information.
Kimsuky has downloaded additional scripts, tools, and malware onto victim systems.
Kimsuky has utilized Native APIs to collect data from victim hosts and facilitate execution of malicious scripts.
Kimsuky has used a proprietary tool to intercept one time passwords required for two-factor authentication.

Kimsuky has modified Registry settings for default file associations to enable all macros and for persistence. Kimsuky has also modified the registry entry for `HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run` registry key for persistence with the name WindowsSecurityCheck.
Kimsuky has captured browser screenshots using TRANSLATEXT. Kimsuky has also obtained screen captures with custom malware.
Kimsuky has used tools such as the MailFetch mail crawler to collect victim emails (excluding spam) from online services via IMAP.
Kimsuky has set auto-forward rules on victim's e-mail accounts.
Kimsuky has the ability to steal data from the clipboard.
Kimsuky has gathered the system time of the device using the PowerShell cmdlet `Get-Date`.
Kimsuky has obfuscated HTTP Post request communications utilizing XOR with a designated key, followed by Base64 encoding.
Kimsuky has used RDP to establish persistence.
Kimsuky has created accounts with net user.

Kimsuky has decoded malicious VBScripts using Base64. Kimsuky has also decoded malicious PowerShell scripts using Base64. Kimsuky has decoded RC4 obfuscated files prior to downloading files from their infrastructure.
Kimsuky has used Google Chrome browser extensions to infect victims and to steal passwords and cookies.
Kimsuky has the ability to use form-grabbing to extract emails and passwords from web data forms.
Kimsuky has exploited various vulnerabilities for initial access, including Microsoft Exchange vulnerability CVE-2020-0688.
Kimsuky has lured victims into clicking malicious links.

Kimsuky has used spearphishing attachments to entice victims into opening malicious files, including LNK files disguised with tailored filenames and fake extensions. Kimsuky has also delivered malicious payloads within archive files (e.g., ZIP), which display decoy documents upon execution while running malicious code in the background.
Kimsuky has leveraged ClickFix type tactics enticing victims to copy and paste malicious code.
Kimsuky has used TRANSLATEXT to redirect clients to legitimate Gmail, Naver or Kakao pages if the clients connect with no parameters.
Kimsuky has collected sensitive browser data using the function `GetBrowserData()` to include login credentials, bookmarks, cookies, and encryption keys.
Kimsuky has used mshta.exe to run malicious scripts on the system.
Kimsuky has executed malware with regsvr32s.
Kimsuky has used `rundll32.exe` to execute malicious scripts and malware on a victim's network.
Kimsuky has used a modified TeamViewer client as a command and control channel.

Kimsuky has utilized a mutex to detect whether its malware is actively running on the victim host. Kimsuky has leveraged PowerShell to store the Process ID (PID) of the currently running malicious PowerShell script into a file named pid.txt which is saved locally on the victim host in the %TEMP% Directory and is queried prior to execution of subsequent PowerShell script to prevent duplication.
Kimsuky has disabled actively running virtual environments using the `KillMe` function to include VMware, Microsoft Hypervisors, and VirtualBox.

Kimsuky has detected and killed virtual environments by using the PowerShell cmdlet `Get-CimInstance` that searches the classname of the computer system manufacturer through an if statement of `if($computerSystem.Manufacturer -match "VMware" -or $computerSystem.Manufacturer -match "Microsoft" -or $computerSystem.Manufacturer -match "VirtualBox")`.
Kimsuky has used modified versions of open source PHP web shells to maintain access, often adding "Dinosaur" references within the code.

Kimsuky has checked for the presence of antivirus software with powershell Get-CimInstance -Namespace root/securityCenter2 – classname antivirusproduct. Kimsuky has also obtained details on antivirus software through WMI queries using `Win32_OperatingSystem` and `SecurityCenter2.AntiVirusProduct`. Kimsuky has also checked the status of Windows Defender through the use `cmd /s sc query WinDefend`.
Kimsuky has sent internal spearphishing emails for lateral movement after stealing victim information.
Kimsuky has used malware, such as TRANSLATEXT, to steal and exfiltrate browser cookies.
Kimsuky has created new services for persistence.
Kimsuky has a HWP document stealer module which changes the default program association in the registry to open HWP documents.
Kimsuky has placed scripts in the startup folder for persistence and modified the `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce` Registry key.
Kimsuky has used pass the hash for authentication to remote access software used in C2.
Kimsuky has used tools that are capable of obtaining credentials from saved mail.
Kimsuky has accessed a Local State files associated with Chromium-based browsers that contain the AES key used to encrypt passwords stored in the browser to include `app_bound_encrypted_key`.
Kimsuky has signed files with the name EGIS CO,. Ltd. and has stolen a valid certificate that is used to sign the malware and the dropper.

Kimsuky has used browser extensions including Google Chrome to steal passwords and cookies from browsers. Kimsuky has also used Nirsoft's WebBrowserPassView tool to dump the passwords obtained from victims.
Kimsuky has used modified versions of PHProxy to examine web traffic between the victim and the accessed website.

Kimsuky has leveraged Component Object Model (COM) to create scheduled tasks to include using naming conventions that mimic legitimate applications. Kimsuky has leveraged obfuscation VBScript to form a string in `WScript.Shell` which has downloaded a malicious payload to the victim environment.

Kimsuky has used QuickZip to archive stolen files before exfiltration. Kimsuky has used the Send() function to compress all collected data into a zip file named init,.zip, then renames it to init.dat, before exfiltration.
Kimsuky has used RC4 encryption before exfil.
Kimsuky has run reg add ‘HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\SpecialAccounts\UserList’ /v to hide a newly created user.
Kimsuky has used an information gathering module that will hide an AV software window from the victim. Kimsuky has also been known to use `-WindowStyle Hidden` to conceal PowerShell windows.
Kimsuky has leveraged the PowerShell `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` command to continue execution through system events.
Kimsuky has used spearphishing to gain initial access and intelligence.

Kimsuky has used emails containing Word, Excel and/or HWP (Hangul Word Processor) documents in their spearphishing campaigns. Kimsuky has also distributed emails with attached compressed zip files that contained malicious .LNK files masquerading as legitimate files. Kimsuky has delivered tailored PDF documents that contain malicious links.
Kimsuky has sent spearphishing emails containing a link to a document that contained malicious macros or took the victim to an actor-controlled domain.
Kimsuky has exfiltrated stolen files and data to actor-controlled Blogspot accounts. Kimsuky has also leveraged Dropbox for uploading victim system information.
Kimsuky has used Dynamic DNS (DDNS) services, such as FreeDNS or No-IP DDNS, to include servers located in South Korea.
Kimsuky has used funds from stolen and laundered cryptocurrency to acquire operational infrastructure.
Kimsuky has registered domains to spoof targeted organizations and trusted third parties including search engines, web platforms, and cryptocurrency exchanges.
Kimsuky has purchased hosting servers with virtual currency and prepaid cards.
Kimsuky has hosted content used for targeting efforts via web services such as Blogspot. Kimsuky has also leveraged Dropbox for hosting payloads and uploading victim system information.
Kimsuky has compromised legitimate sites and used them to distribute malware.
Kimsuky has leveraged stolen PII to create accounts.
Kimsuky has created social media accounts to monitor news and security trends as well as potential targets.
Kimsuky has created email accounts for phishing operations.
Kimsuky has compromised email accounts to send spearphishing e-mails.
Kimsuky created and used a mailing toolkit to use in spearphishing attacks.
Kimsuky has developed its own unique malware such as MailFetch.py for use in operations.
Kimsuky has obtained and used tools such as Nirsoft WebBrowserPassVIew, Mimikatz, and PsExec.
Kimsuky has stolen a valid certificate that is used to sign the malware and the dropper.
Kimsuky has obtained exploit code for various CVEs.
Kimsuky has collected valid email addresses including personal accounts that were subsequently used for spearphishing and other forms of social engineering.
Kimsuky has collected victim employee name information.

Kimsuky has collected victim organization information including but not limited to organization hierarchy, functions, press releases, and others. Kimsuky has also used large language models (LLMs) to gather information about potential targets of interest.
Kimsuky has used Twitter to monitor potential victims and to prepare targeted phishing e-mails.
Kimsuky has searched for vulnerabilities, tools, and geopolitical trends on Google to target victims.
Kimsuky has searched for information on the target company's website.
Kimsuky has used LLMs to better understand publicly reported vulnerabilities.
Kimsuky has used tailored spearphishing emails to gather victim information including contat lists to identify additional targets.

Kimsuky has used links in e-mail to steal account information including web beacons for target profiling. Kimsuky has also utilized QR codes (also known as Quishing) to direct victims to malicious links through the reliance of a mobile device to scan a code with an embedded malicious URL.

Kimsuky has used compromised and acquired infrastructure to host and deliver malware including Blogspot to host beacons, file exfiltrators, and implants. Kimsuky has also hosted malicious payloads on Dropbox.

Kimsuky has used the Invoke-Mimikatz PowerShell script to reflectively load a Mimikatz credential stealing DLL into memory. Kimsuky has also used reflective loading through .NET assembly using `[System.Reflection.Assembly]::Load`.
Kimsuky has stolen and laundered cryptocurrency to self-fund operations including the acquisition of infrastructure.
Kimsuky has utilized the Sleep function to ensure execution of scripts.
Kimsuky has enumerated drives.
Kimsuky has used LLMs to identify think tanks, government organizations, and experts to inform targeting for spearphishing campaigns.

Kimsuky has also impersonated legitimate people, such as a foreign advisor, an embassy employee, and a think tank employee. Kimsuky has also purported to be a Japanese diplomat to communicate with the victims.
Kimsuky has been observed turning off Windows Security Center and can hide the AV software window from the view of the infected user.
Kimsuky has been observed disabling the system firewall.

ctx.desc: Kimsuky is a Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK)-based cyber espionage group that has been active since at least 2012. The group initially targeted South Korean government agencies, think tanks, and subject-matter experts in various fields. Its operations expanded to include the United Nations and organizations in the government, education, business services, and manufacturing sectors across the United States, Japan, Russia, and Europe.

G1049.d: AppleJeus is a North Korean state-sponsored threat group attributed to the Reconnaissance General Bureau. Associated with the broader Lazarus Group umbrella of actors, AppleJeus has been active since at least 2018 and is closely aligned in resources with TEMP.hermit, another DPRK-affiliated group under the same umbrella. The group’s primary mission is to generate and launder revenue to provide financial support to the government. AppleJeus primarily targets the cryptocurrency industry and is most notably responsible for the 3CX Supply Chain Attack. The group traditionally deploys malicious cryptocurrency software in combination with Phishing. From these compromised environments, it selectively deploys additional backdoors to enable extended operations against high-value financial targets.
contrib: Austin Larsen and the Google Threat Intelligence Group

G1017.d:
Volt Typhoon is a People's Republic of China (PRC) state-sponsored actor that has been active since at least 2021, primarily targeting critical infrastructure organizations in the US and its territories including Guam. Volt Typhoon's targeting and pattern of behavior have been assessed as pre-positioning to enable lateral movement to operational technology (OT) assets for potential destructive or disruptive attacks. Volt Typhoon has emphasized stealth in operations using web shells, living-off-the-land (LOTL) binaries, hands on keyboard activities, and stolen credentials.. The group has leveraged compromised SOHO routers to proxy command and control traffic and obscure its infrastructure, activity associated with the KV botnet.. 

Reporting indicates a separate initial access cluster, SYLVANITE, has been observed exploiting internet-facing edge devices and transferring access to Volt Typhoon, also tracked as VOLTZITE, for follow-on operations.

ctx.desc: Volt Typhoon is a People's Republic of China (PRC) state-sponsored actor that has been active since at least 2021, primarily targeting critical infrastructure organizations in the US and its territories including Guam. Volt Typhoon's targeting and pattern of behavior have been assessed as pre-positioning to enable lateral movement to operational technology (OT) assets for potential destructive or disruptive attacks. Volt Typhoon has emphasized stealth in operations using web shells, living-off-the-land (LOTL) binaries, hands on keyboard activities, and stolen credentials..

G0040.d: Patchwork is a cyber espionage group that was first observed in December 2015. While the group has not been definitively attributed, circumstantial evidence suggests the group may be a pro-Indian or Indian entity. Patchwork has been seen targeting industries related to diplomatic and government agencies. Much of the code used by this group was copied and pasted from online forums. Patchwork was also seen operating spearphishing campaigns targeting U.S. think tank groups in March and April of 2018.

pr.p: Patchwork collected and exfiltrated files from the infected system.
Patchwork attempted to use RDP to move laterally.
Patchwork apparently altered NDiskMonitor samples by adding four bytes of random letters in a likely attempt to change the file hashes.
A Patchwork payload was packed with UPX.
Patchwork apparently altered NDiskMonitor samples by adding four bytes of random letters in a likely attempt to change the file hashes.
Patchwork has obfuscated a script with Crypto Obfuscator.
Patchwork collected the victim username and whether it was running as admin, then sent the information to its C2 server.

tech.n: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

pr.p: Patchwork installed its payload in the startup programs folder as "Baidu Software Update." The group also adds its second stage payload to the startup programs as “Net Monitor." They have also dropped QuasarRAT binaries as files named microsoft_network.exe and crome.exe.
A Patchwork file stealer can run a TaskScheduler DLL to add persistence.
A Patchwork payload uses process hollowing to hide the UAC bypass vulnerability exploitation inside svchost.exe.
Patchwork used PowerSploit to download payloads, run a reverse shell, and execute malware on the victim's machine.
Patchwork ran a reverse shell with Meterpreter. Patchwork used JavaScript code and .SCT files on victim machines.
Patchwork used Visual Basic Scripts (VBS) on victim machines.
Patchwork removed certain files and replaced them so they could not be retrieved.
Patchwork copied all targeted files to a directory called index that was eventually uploaded to the C&C server.
Patchwork collected the victim computer name, OS version, and architecture type and sent the information to its C2 server.
A Patchwork payload has searched all fixed drives on the victim for files matching a specified list of extensions.
Patchwork hides base64-encoded and encrypted C2 server locations in comments on legitimate websites.
Patchwork payloads download additional files from the C2 server.
A Patchwork payload deletes Resiliency Registry keys created by Microsoft Office applications in an apparent effort to trick users into thinking there were no issues during application runs.

Patchwork developed a file stealer to search C:\ and collect files with certain extensions. Patchwork also executed a script to enumerate all drives, store them as a list, and upload generated files to the C2 server.
Patchwork used Base64 to encode C2 traffic.
Patchwork has used watering holes to deliver files with exploits to initial victims.
Patchwork has used BITS jobs to download malicious payloads.

Patchwork uses malicious documents to deliver remote execution exploits as part of. The group has previously exploited CVE-2017-8570, CVE-2012-1856, CVE-2014-4114, CVE-2017-0199, CVE-2017-11882, and CVE-2015-1641.
Patchwork has used spearphishing with links to try to get users to click, download and open malicious files.
Patchwork embedded a malicious macro in a Word document and lured the victim to click on an icon to execute the malware.
Patchwork scanned the “Program Files” directories for a directory with the string “Total Security” (the installation path of the “360 Total Security” antivirus tool).
Patchwork has added the path of its second-stage malware to the startup folder to achieve persistence. One of its file stealers has also persisted by adding a Registry Run key.
Patchwork bypassed User Access Control (UAC).
Patchwork has signed malware with self-signed certificates from fictitious and spoofed legitimate software companies.
Patchwork dumped the login data database from \AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Login Data.
Patchwork leveraged the DDE protocol to deliver their malware.
Patchwork encrypted the collected files' path with AES and then encoded them with base64.
Patchwork has used spearphishing with an attachment to deliver files with exploits to initial victims.
Patchwork has used spearphishing with links to deliver files with exploits to initial victims.
A Patchwork .dll that contains BADNEWS is loaded and executed using DLL side-loading.
Patchwork has created self-signed certificates from fictitious and spoofed legitimate software companies that were later used to sign malware.
Patchwork has obtained and used open-source tools such as QuasarRAT.
Patchwork has used embedded image tags (known as web bugs) with unique, per-recipient tracking links in their emails for the purpose of identifying which recipients opened messages.
Patchwork enumerated all available drives on the victim's machine.

G0096.d: APT41 is a threat group that researchers have assessed as Chinese state-sponsored espionage group that also conducts financially-motivated operations. Active since at least 2012, APT41 has been observed targeting various industries, including but not limited to healthcare, telecom, technology, finance, education, retail and video game industries in 14 countries. Notable behaviors include using a wide range of malware and tools to complete mission objectives. APT41 overlaps at least partially with public reporting on groups including BARIUM and Winnti Group.

pr.p: APT41 has used hashdump, Mimikatz, Procdump, and the Windows Credential Editor to dump password hashes from memory and authenticate to other user accounts.
APT41 extracted user account data from the Security Account Managerr (SAM), making a copy of this database from the registry using the reg save command or by exploiting volume shadow copies.
APT41 used ntdsutil to obtain a copy of the victim environment ntds.dit file.
APT41 has uploaded files and data from a compromised host.
APT41 used the Steam community page as a fallback mechanism for C2.
APT41 queried registry values to determine items such as configured RDP ports and network configurations.
APT41 deployed rootkits on Linux systems.
APT41 collected MAC addresses from victim machines.
APT41 has used MiPing to discover active systems in the victim network.
APT41 used RDP for lateral movement. APT41 used NATBypass to expose local RDP ports on compromised systems to the Internet.
APT41 has transferred implant files using Windows Admin Shares and the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol, then executes files through Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI).
APT41 used VMProtected binaries in multiple intrusions.
APT41 uses packers such as Themida to obfuscate malicious files.
APT41 transfers post-exploitation files dividing the payload into fixed-size chunks to evade detection.
APT41 has executed whoami commands, including using the WMIEXEC utility to execute this on remote machines.
APT41 has created services to appear as benign system tools.

pr.p: APT41 attempted to masquerade their files as popular anti-virus software.
APT41 used a hidden shell script in `/etc/rc.d/init.d` to leverage the `ADORE.XSEC`backdoor and `Adore-NG` rootkit.
APT41 used a malware variant called WIDETONE to conduct port scans on specified subnets.
APT41 used WMI in several ways, including for execution of commands via WMIEXEC as well as for persistence via PowerSploit. APT41 has executed files through Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI).

APT41 has enumerated IP addresses of network resources and used the netstat command as part of network reconnaissance. The group has also used a malware variant, HIGHNOON, to enumerate active RDP sessions.
APT41 used a compromised account to create a scheduled task on a system.
APT41 malware TIDYELF loaded the main WINTERLOVE component by injecting it into the iexplore.exe process.
APT41 used a keylogger called GEARSHIFT on a target system.
APT41 leveraged PowerShell to deploy malware families in victims’ environments.

APT41 used cmd.exe /c to execute commands on remote machines.
APT41 used a batch file to install persistence for the Cobalt Strike BEACON loader.
APT41 used Linux shell commands for system survey and information gathering prior to exploitation of vulnerabilities such as CVE-2019-19871.
APT41 used net group commands to enumerate various Windows user groups and permissions.
APT41 attempted to remove evidence of some of its activity by deleting Bash histories.
APT41 deleted files from the system.
APT41 used HTTP to download payloads for CVE-2019-19781 and CVE-2020-10189 exploits.
APT41 used exploit payloads that initiate download via ftp.
APT41 used DNS for C2 communications.
APT41 used compromised credentials to log on to other systems.
APT41 uses multiple built-in commands such as systeminfo and `net config Workstation` to enumerate victim system basic configuration information.
APT41 has executed file /bin/pwd on exploited victims, perhaps to return architecture related information.
APT41 used built-in net commands to enumerate local administrator groups.
APT41 used built-in net commands to enumerate domain administrator users.
APT41 used a tool called CLASSFON to covertly proxy network communications.
APT41 has added user accounts to the User and Admin groups.
APT41 used legitimate websites for C2 through dead drop resolvers (DDR), including GitHub, Pastebin, and Microsoft TechNet.
APT41 used the storescyncsvc.dll BEACON backdoor to download a secondary backdoor.

APT41 used certutil to download additional files. APT41 downloaded post-exploitation tools such as Cobalt Strike via command shell following initial access. APT41 has uploaded Procdump and NATBypass to a staging directory and has used these tools in follow-on activities.
APT41 performed password brute-force attacks on the local admin account.
APT41 used a malware variant called GOODLUCK to modify the registry in order to steal credentials.
APT41 compromised an online billing/payment service using VPN access between a third-party service provider and the targeted payment service.
APT41 used the net share command as part of network reconnaissance.
APT41 has created user accounts.

APT41 exploited CVE-2020-10189 against Zoho ManageEngine Desktop Central through unsafe deserialization, and CVE-2019-19781 to compromise Citrix Application Delivery Controllers (ADC) and gateway devices. APT41 leveraged vulnerabilities such as ProxyLogon exploitation or SQL injection for initial access. APT41 exploited CVE-2021-26855 against a vulnerable Microsoft Exchange Server to gain initial access to the victim network.
APT41 gained access to production environments where they could inject malicious code into legitimate, signed files and widely distribute them to end users.
APT41 used BITSAdmin to download and install payloads.
APT41 leveraged the follow exploits in their operations: CVE-2012-0158, CVE-2015-1641, CVE-2017-0199, CVE-2017-11882, and CVE-2019-3396.
APT41 cloned victim user Git repositories during intrusions.
APT41 used compiled HTML (.chm) files for targeting.
APT41 has used rundll32.exe to execute a loader.

APT41 has encrypted payloads using the Data Protection API (DPAPI), which relies on keys tied to specific user accounts on specific machines. APT41 has also environmentally keyed second stage malware with an RC5 key derived in part from the infected system's volume serial number.
APT41 used scheduled tasks created via Group Policy Objects (GPOs) to deploy ransomware.

APT41 used a ransomware called Encryptor RaaS to encrypt files on the targeted systems and provide a ransom note to the user. APT41 also used Microsoft Bitlocker to encrypt workstations and Jetico’s BestCrypt to encrypt servers.
APT41 deployed a Monero cryptocurrency mining tool in a victim’s environment.
APT41 deployed Master Boot Record bootkits on Windows systems to hide their malware and maintain persistence on victim systems.
APT41 modified legitimate Windows services to install malware backdoors. APT41 created the StorSyncSvc service to provide persistence for Cobalt Strike.
APT41 leveraged sticky keys to establish persistence.
APT41 created and modified startup files for persistence. APT41 added a registry key in HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Svchost to establish persistence for Cobalt Strike.
APT41 uses tools such as Mimikatz to enable lateral movement via captured password hashes.
APT41 leveraged code-signing certificates to sign malware when targeting both gaming and non-gaming organizations.
APT41 has obtained information about accounts, lists of employees, and plaintext and hashed passwords from databases.
APT41 used BrowserGhost, a tool designed to obtain credentials from browsers, to retrieve information from password stores.

APT41 created a RAR archive of targeted files for exfiltration. Additionally, APT41 used the makecab.exe utility to both download tools, such as NATBypass, to the victim network and to archive a file for exfiltration.
APT41 sent spearphishing emails with attachments such as compiled HTML (.chm) files to initially compromise their victims.
APT41 has used DGAs to change their C2 servers monthly.
APT41 used svchost.exe and Net to execute a system service installed to launch a Cobalt Strike BEACON loader.
APT41 uses remote shares to move and remotely execute payloads during lateral movemement.
APT41 has used search order hijacking to execute malicious payloads, such as Winnti for Windows. APT41 has also used legitimate executables to perform DLL side-loading of their malware.
APT41 has configured payloads to load via LD_PRELOAD.
APT41 has obtained and used tools such as Mimikatz, pwdump, PowerSploit, and Windows Credential Editor.
APT41 used the Acunetix SQL injection vulnerability scanner in target reconnaissance operations, as well as the JexBoss tool to identify vulnerabilities in Java applications.
APT41 leverages various tools and frameworks to brute-force directories on web servers.
APT41 uses the Chinese website fofa.su, similar to the Shodan scanning service, for passive scanning of victims.
APT41 used `NATBypass` to bypass firewall restrictions and to access compromised systems via RDP.
APT41 impersonated an employee at a video game developer company to send phishing emails.
APT41 developed a custom injector that enables an Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) bypass, making malicious processes invisible to Windows logging.
APT41 attempted to remove evidence of some of its activity by clearing Windows security and system events.

sw.p: APT41 used a variant of PlugX to connect to Windows and Linux systems via SSH and Samba/CIFS.
DUSTTRAP is used by APT41.
APT41 used Impacket to dump LSA secrets on one of the domain controllers in the victim network.
APT41 used the `China Chopper` web shell as a persistence mechanism on compromised Microsoft Exchange servers.
DUSTPAN has been used by APT41 in various campaigns since at least 2021.

APT41 DUST targeted sectors such as shipping, logistics, and media for information gathering purposes. APT41 used previously-observed malware such as DUSTPAN as well as newly observed tool

Active since at least 2012, APT41 has been observed targeting various industries, including but not limited to healthcare, telecom, technology, finance, education, retail and video game industries in 14 countries. Notable behaviors include using a wide range of malware and tools to complete mission objectives.

G1045.d: Salt Typhoon is a People's Republic of China (PRC) state-backed actor that has been active since at least 2019 and responsible for numerous compromises of network infrastructure at major U.S. telecommunication and internet service providers (ISP). Salt Typhoon has targeted and leveraged public facing network edge devices to gain access to victim environments. Salt Typhoon has been publicly associated with activities resembling other security industry reported activity groups to include OPERATOR PANDA, RedMike, GhostEmperor, and UNC5807.

pr.p: Salt Typhoon has gathered data from victim devices.
Salt Typhoon has discovered and modified network configurations of victim devices.
Salt Typhoon has used SNMPwalk to enumerate devices.
Salt Typhoon has enabled traffic mirroring to exfiltrate data.
Salt Typhoon has opened and conducted operations utilizing RDP within victim environments.

Salt Typhoon has modified the loopback address on compromised switches and used them as the source of SSH connections to additional devices within the target environment, allowing them to bypass access control lists (ACLs). Salt Typhoon has also enabled SSH to allow remote access.
Salt Typhoon has obfuscated target pathways with double encoding to bypass security solutions.
Salt Typhoon has used a variety of tools and techniques to capture packet data between network interfaces.
Salt Typhoon has scanned open ports and services within the victim environment.
Salt Typhoon has exfiltrated configuration files from exploited network devices over FTP and TFTP.
Salt Typhoon has utilized a bash shell to execute Linux commands.
Salt Typhoon has used Python scripts to execute commands on victim hosts.

Salt Typhoon has executed commands on network devices using the native command line interface. 

Salt Typhoon has leveraged Tcl scripts on Cisco IOS devices to include `TCLprox.tcl` and `map.tcl` when `tclsh` was available. 

Salt Typhoon also leveraged TACACS+ and RADIUS to modify victim network devices.
Salt Typhoon has leveraged Cisco Guest Shell to interact with a Linux Container on network devices.
Salt Typhoon has deleted and cleared logs to avoid detection.

tech.n: Clear Network Connection History and Configurations

pr.p: Salt Typhoon has reverted or modified network configuration files to remove traces of activity.

Salt Typhoon has removed persistence within victim devices through disabling and uninstalling artifacts. 
Salt Typhoon has leveraged the commands `guestshell disable` and `guestshell destroy` to deactivate and uninstall Guest Shell containers and return all resources to the system to remove evidence of persistence.
Salt Typhoon has utilized HTTP and HTTPS in C2 communications.
Salt Typhoon has leveraged SFTP for C2 communications.
Salt Typhoon has abused network management tools to include RANCID to facilitate actions in victims’ environments.
Salt Typhoon has used logged into accounts on Cisco devices by cracking weak hashed passwords from configuration files.
Salt Typhoon has discovered system information details utilizing CLI on network devices.
Salt Typhoon has utilized virtual private servers and compromised routers as proxies for malicious communications.
Salt Typhoon has leveraged multi-hop proxies for command-and-control infrastructure.
Salt Typhoon has used Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) and IPsec tunnels to connect to C2 over non-application layer protocols.
Salt Typhoon has added SSH authorized_keys under root or other users at the Linux level on compromised network devices.
Salt Typhoon has downloaded additional payloads and files to victim devices.
Salt Typhoon has used weak credentials to gain access to victim devices.

Salt Typhoon has cracked passwords for accounts with weak encryption obtained from the configuration files of compromised network devices.

Salt Typhoon has cracked weak hashed passwords stolen from configuration files.
Salt Typhoon has utilized double encoding with hexadecimals in attempts to obfuscate requested command paths.
Salt Typhoon has created Linux-level users on compromised network devices through modification of `/etc/shadow` and `/etc/passwd`.

Salt Typhoon has created local user accounts to utilize in victim environments. 

Salt Typhoon has also created administrative accounts within compromised environments.

Salt Typhoon has leveraged vulnerabilities in public facing applications and network edge devices including Cisco IOS and IOS XE through CVE-2018-0171, Ivanti Connect Secure through CVE-2023-46805, and Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect through CVE-2024-3400.

Salt Typhoon has leveraged compromised devices associated with trusted connections or those associated with private interconnections to include provider-to-provider or provider-to-customer relationships in order to pivot to target networks.
Salt Typhoon has modified container service configurations using `Guest Shell`.
Salt Typhoon has elevated privileges of local user accounts by editing `/etc/sudoers` or adding a file under `/etc/sudoers.d/`.
Salt Typhoon has collected credentials stored in configuration files.

Salt Typhoon has modified the Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) configurations forcing devices to use less secure authentication methods and to send information to their infrastructure.
Salt Typhoon has utilized SNMP daemon to execute commands to include SNMPwalk.
Salt Typhoon has leveraged non-standard ports to evade detection by security monitoring.
Salt Typhoon has modified device configurations to create and use Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) tunnels.
Salt Typhoon has utilized virtual private servers (VPS) for C2 infrastructure.
Salt Typhoon has leveraged compromised routers to facilitate operations.
Salt Typhoon members have created and maintained professional accounts on social media to include LinkedIn.
Salt Typhoon has hosted and attended formal training programs for foreign-made IT products to include Cisco Network Academy.
Salt Typhoon has used custom tooling including JumbledPath.

Salt Typhoon has used publicly available tooling to exploit vulnerabilities.

Salt Typhoon has also obtained and utilized open-source tools for creating backdoors and multi-hop proxies to include STOWAWAY.
Salt Typhoon has obtained and utilized numerous exploits that target network edge devices to include Cisco IOS, Palo Alto Pan-OS Global Protect, and Ivanti Connect Secure.
Salt Typhoon has used configuration files from exploited network devices to help discover upstream and downstream network segments.
Salt Typhoon has scanned victim environments for open ports and services.
Salt Typhoon has abused peer connections to exfiltrate data.
Salt Typhoon has enumerated device configuration using SNMP and gathered data stored in the Managed Information Base on target devices.
Salt Typhoon has attempted to acquire credentials by dumping network device configurations. Salt Typhoon has also obtained data using RANCID.
Salt Typhoon has enabled Linux containers in victim network device environments using `guestshell enable`.
Salt Typhoon has disabled logging and disabled the distribution of logs to log aggregators.

tech.n: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs

pr.p: Salt Typhoon has cleared logs including .bash_history, auth.log, lastlog, wtmp, and btmp.
Salt Typhoon has made changes to the Access Control List (ACL) and loopback interface address on compromised devices.
Salt Typhoon has modified the network firewalls access control lists to add IP addresses to bypass security policies and maintain access.
